extracted.intended_audience: educated London readers; critics, playwrights, actors, and readers of The Spectator
extracted.subtask_description: Normative guidance and evaluative criteria for literary criticism and theatrical writing/representation, with allied remarks on forms of government and public life as they bear on taste and morals. Aimed at judges of poetry/drama, playwrights, actors, and cultivated readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonableness of government
rubrics_metrics.description: The most reasonable form of government is that which is most conformable to the equality found in human nature, so long as it is consistent with public peace and tranquility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liberty is exemption from subjection so far as the order and economy of government will permit; therefore a constitution should safeguard individual liberty while maintaining public order. Evaluate governments by how well they reconcile human equality with public tranquillity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal rather than partial liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: Liberty should reach every individual of a people; if it only spreads among particular branches, there had better be none at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partial liberties amplify the misfortune of those deprived of them by creating disagreeable comparisons. Prefer systems that extend rights broadly rather than privileging narrow groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative plurality and balance of powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislative power is best lodged in several persons, especially of different ranks and interests; a mixed government of three branches (regal, noble, popular) is pre-eminent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One legislative body tends to tyranny; two bodies lack a casting voice and invite disputes; four causes confusion. Use historical models (Polybius, Cicero, Roman Commonwealth vs English constitution) as examples. Assess constitutions by number and functional distribution of legislative organs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of varied interests among legislators
rubrics_metrics.description: The greatest security for liberty occurs when legislators are so distinguished that by providing for the particular interests of their several ranks they provide for the whole body of the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer arrangements where every part of the people has a common interest with at least one part of the legislature. Evaluate whether legislators' interests align with and protect subordinate groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid relying on absolute rulers (anti-despotism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Relying on the virtue of a single absolute ruler is dangerous because power commonly corrupts; history shows many tyrants and many good heirs become cruel when absolute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not design government to depend on chance virtues of an individual. Consider empirical evidence about how power extinguishes fear and moral restraint; prefer institutional checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic foundations for learning and the arts
rubrics_metrics.description: Riches and plenty are the natural fruits of liberty, and where these abound learning and the liberal arts immediately lift up their heads and flourish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess cultural flourishing in light of material conditions: competence with necessities, ease, and plenty encourage speculation, study, and the diffusion of arts. Despotic governments that produce poverty are less likely to sustain learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not model earthly government on a presumed divine monarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: Making our governments on earth like that in heaven (monarchical and unlimited) is ill-advised unless the human ruler matches the Creator in goodness and justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prudence counsels institutional limits because human rulers lack divine perfection. Use moral reasoning about human fallibility when judging desired scope of executive power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy should represent truth and humane life
rubrics_metrics.description: A good tragedy represents truth and humane life in incidents concerning heroes and heroines; the passions should be genuine and founded on high conceptions of virtue and merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer plays where characters' sorrows arise from noble motives or unguarded virtue rather than mere weakness or affectation. Example: The Distressed Mother praised for producing real tears and humane passion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grandeur of character expressed by sentiments, not stage ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: To make a character truly great, the author should give it a foundation in superior thoughts and maxims of conduct; grandeur appears in greatness of sentiment rather than in ostentatious stage trappings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid conveying social status by superfluous props or attendants; convey it through elevated thought and conduct. Evaluate characters by their inner moral and intellectual stature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect decency, honour, and good-breeding in representation of sorrow
rubrics_metrics.description: Passion, sorrow, indignation, and even despair ought to be represented within the rules of decency, honour, and good-breeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audiences should see sorrow presented in a manner they can imitate or learn from; unchecked or scandalous displays that violate decorum are to be avoided in decent tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stagecraft should match audience taste and avoid needless bustle
rubrics_metrics.description: Plays should be sufficiently ‘busy’ for present taste but not at the cost of natural representation; scenes should be handled carefully and parts appropriately dressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical stage advice: ensure scenes engage current audiences, but keep the author's naturalness and integrity. Avoid over-crowding or unnecessary attendants; refresh costumes (every part perfectly new dressed) if that suits public taste, but not at the cost of nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: The critic must be broadly learned
rubrics_metrics.description: A critic ought not to be acquainted only with French and Italian critics but also with ancient and modern writers, especially Greek and Latin poets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior study across languages and traditions provides the background lights needed to understand and judge criticism. Lack of such learning often leads to misinterpretation and mistaken judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical clarity and ability to distinguish words from things
rubrics_metrics.description: A critic must have a clear and logical head and the art of distinguishing between words and things; otherwise his ideas are confused and obscure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training in logic (Aristotle cited) and Locke's distinction between names and things are important prerequisites. Evaluate critics by their capacity to organize thoughts and convey them with perspicuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Praise excellencies rather than fixating on faults
rubrics_metrics.description: A true critic should dwell upon the excellencies of a writer, discover concealed beauties, and communicate what is worth readers' observation rather than hunting for little faults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the popular tendency to expose surface errors only. Remember Dryden's injunction: those who would search for pearls must dive below. Criticism should reveal and elucidate beauty, not merely ridicule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ridicule and misplaced wit in criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Using wit improperly, especially turning a glowing expression into ridicule, is unseasonable and prejudicial in criticism; a 'gift of ridicule' leads to unfair attacks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism should have a serious and instructive air; satire and merriment are inappropriate when they simply show off the critic's cleverness at the expense of fair judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnosing poor critics and common anti-patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlearned or superficial critics often only praise what has been publicly applauded, focus solely on little faults, and adopt a few general rules or cant from foreign critics to appear judicious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of critics who rely on received opinion, ridicule popular targets, or mimic French formulas without deep learning. Such critics are exposed by their habit of attacking 'verbum ardens' and little strokes of genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer works of great genius with lapses to flawless mediocrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Productions of great genius, even with many lapses and inadvertencies, are infinitely preferable to the works of inferior authors that are scrupulously exact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating major poets (e.g., Milton), weigh the magnitude of genius and overarching excellence more heavily than minor faults of execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: History: the deaths of eminent persons are most affecting and instructive
rubrics_metrics.description: Accounts of the deaths of eminent persons and their behavior in that dreadful season are among the most improving and affecting parts of history, because death is a universal circumstance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical narratives gain moral weight and reader interest when they include sincere accounts of dying and final conduct; such episodes speak to all readers and encourage reflection on mortality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social norm for visitors among families with young females (on jilts/fribblers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Visitors who frequent families with young females should either declare themselves (their intentions) or absent themselves; indecisive men (fribblers) who profess passion but dread consent are harmful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parents should not wink at ambiguous addresses; require a clear account of appearances and timely declarations to prevent emotional harm to young women. This is presented as a moral/social prescription rather than a literary rule.
